summary: For ages 7–9, explain why the poles have extreme seasons: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5° and points in a FIXED direction as Earth orbits the Sun, so each pole spends half the year leaning toward the Sun (continuous daylight, comparatively warmer summer) and half leaning away (continuous darkness, bitter winter). The seasons come from the tilt, not from Earth's changing distance to the Sun. The same tilt drives sea ice expanding in winter and retreating in summer, and animal cycles of migration and breeding. The preferred build is a 2D orbit a child can drag to see which pole is lit, with linked day/night and sea-ice responses; a 3D fly-around orbit, a tap-to-reveal static diagram, a torch-and-globe demonstration, and targeted multiple-choice checks are offered as alternatives with different purposes, none claimed to be superior.
misconceptions: Seasons happen because Earth moves closer to and further from the Sun — it's the axial TILT, not distance
The whole Earth is hot in summer and cold in winter at once — opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons
The axis tips back and forth toward the Sun — it points a fixed direction; Earth's position in orbit changes which pole leans sunward
The Sun goes out in polar winter — that pole is tilted away, so the Sun stays below the horizon
Seasons and sea-ice/animal cycles are unrelated — the same tilt drives the extreme seasons AND the yearly ice and migration cycles

activities.title: Drag Earth around the Sun with a fixed tilt
steps: Grab Earth and drag it all the way around a glowing Sun, noticing that the axis stays locked pointing the same direction for the whole loop.
Watch a spotlight show which pole is bathed in sunlight as Earth moves.

Drag Earth to the position where the North Pole leans into the light and observe a day-clock spinning a full 24 hours with the Sun never setting (Arctic summer, midnight sun) while a sea-ice gauge shrinks.
Drag Earth to the opposite side where the North Pole leans away and observe the Sun never rising, the polar-night scene darkening, and the sea-ice gauge growing.
State in your own words which pole has summer at each position and why.

Use a 'blame the distance?' toggle that briefly moves Earth slightly nearer and further and notice that, in this simplified model, the seasons do not change. In real life, the small change in distance has only a minor effect and is not what causes the seasons.
activities.insight: The SAME fixed tilt produces summer on one side of the orbit and winter on the other; it is the tilt (combined with orbital position), not distance to the Sun, that makes a pole swing between endless day and endless night.

activities.title: Fly around the orbit in 3D to find the sunward-leaning pole
steps: Move your viewpoint around a 3D Earth-Sun orbit to look at the tilted axis from different angles.

At each of four orbital positions, identify which pole is leaning toward the Sun and which is leaning away. Notice that at the two in-between (equinox) positions, neither pole leans toward the Sun, and both poles get some day and some night.
At the two positions where one pole leans fully toward the Sun, describe how the lit pole experiences continuous daylight and the dark pole continuous night.
activities.insight: Earth-Sun geometry is genuinely three-dimensional; viewing the tilt from different angles can build spatial intuition for why one pole is bathed in light while the other is in darkness.

activities.title: Four-position orbit diagram with tap-to-reveal labels
steps: Look at an orbit diagram showing Earth at four positions with its axis drawn in a fixed direction.
Tap each position to reveal whether the North Pole leans toward the Sun, away from it, or neither (sideways to the Sun, at the spring and autumn positions), and the season it causes.
Match each position to 'summer/midnight-sun', 'winter/polar-night' or 'spring/autumn (in-between, with sunrise and sunset)' for the North Pole.
activities.insight: At different points in the same orbit, the fixed tilt leaves one pole leaning sunward (summer) and later leaning away (winter).

activities.title: Torch-and-tilted-globe demonstration
steps: Tilt a globe so its axis points a fixed direction, then carry it around a torch standing in for the Sun, keeping the tilt pointing the same way the whole time.
Spin the globe at the position where one pole leans toward the torch and watch that pole stay in the light through a full spin (midnight sun).
Carry the globe to the opposite side and spin it again to see that pole stay in shadow (polar night).
Describe what season each pole is having at each position.
activities.insight: A pole tilted toward the light source stays lit even as Earth spins, giving continuous daylight; a pole tilted away stays dark, giving continuous night.

activities.title: Check understanding: tilt vs distance and which pole has summer
steps: Answer which-pole-has-summer questions for given orbital positions.
Decide whether tilt or distance explains the seasons, using the fact that opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.
Explain how the same tilt links to sea ice spreading in winter and shrinking in summer, and to animal migration or breeding on the yearly cycle.
activities.insight: A learner who understands credits the axial tilt (not distance) and can connect the seasonal cycle to at least one consequence such as sea-ice change or animal behaviour.

checkQuestion: The poles have extreme seasons — a summer of endless daylight, a winter of endless dark. A student says 'that's because in summer the Earth is much CLOSER to the Sun, and in winter it's much farther away.' Is it distance from the Sun that causes the seasons? If not, what does — and why does that give a pole months of daylight then months of dark?
checkAnswer: No — seasons are NOT caused by the Earth getting closer to or farther from the Sun. They are caused by the TILT of the Earth's axis (about 23.5°). As the Earth orbits the Sun, each pole spends half the year tilted TOWARD the Sun — giving continuous daylight and the warmer polar summer — and half tilted AWAY — giving continuous darkness and bitter winter. (In fact both hemispheres are at similar distances from the Sun at the same time, and it's the tilt, not distance, that gives one summer while the other has winter.) The same tilt drives sea ice growing in winter and shrinking in summer, and animal behaviours like migration and breeding.
